title: Latency-tiered placement and residency routing for Dedicated fleets
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Problem: Customers with Dedicated capacity want deterministic latency guarantees and strict data residency, but current placement is either region-first or zone-first with coarse controls. When traffic spikes or zones are drained, requests can be routed to farther racks that violate latency budgets or residency constraints.

Goal: Implement a tiered placement policy and residency-aware routing layer that prioritizes low-latency candidate pools within residency bounds, exposes explicit throughput reservation tiers, and gracefully expands the candidate set under pressure while keeping customers within declared residency and SLA obligations.
acceptance_criteria: Policy engine supports latency tiers: local-zone, local-region, allowed-region (soft), fallback-global (only for non-residency customers)
Routing respects residency flags (country/region labels) and blocks routes that would violate customer residency when configured
Throughput reservation tiers exposed in API with explicit guarantees and measurable SLOs
Autoscaler can vertically expand candidate set following tier order and fall back only when lower tiers are exhausted
Integration tests simulate zone drain and show failover preserves SLA for P99 latency within defined thresholds for 95% of requests
Documentation and Console controls for admins to set residency policy, latency SLAs, and reserved throughput per tier
design_notes: Introduce Placement Tier abstraction: each tier is an ordered set of placement rules (zone affinity, region affinity, latency budget, residency label predicates)
Attach residency label metadata to fleet membership at provisioning time and surface via fleet descriptors (country_code, region_code)
Routing decision flow: evaluate candidate tiers in order, filter by residency, compute estimated tail latency using recent telemetry, pick best candidate satisfying throughput headroom
Throughput reservations implemented as lease tokens on pool allocators; reservation tiers consume tokens before burst capacity
Autoscaler extension: policy-driven expansion that can add nodes from allowed-region pools when local pools are saturated; expansion must respect residency_or_strict flag
Configuration API: new fields in Dedicated Fleet spec: placement_tiers (ordered), residency_mode (strict|preferred|none), reserved_units_by_tier, latency_budget_ms
implementation_plan: Week 1: Schema changes for fleet descriptors and API (fleet service + console config UI)
Week 2: Placement tier proto and local decision engine in router; unit tests for filtering logic
Week 3: Integrate telemetry (P50/P95/P99) into routing score and add reservation token mechanics to pool allocator
Week 4: Autoscaler policy hooks to expand candidate set by tier, implement safe-drain simulation and soft-failover path
Week 5: End-to-end integration tests (multi-zone simulation), create migration tool for existing fleets
Week 6: Docs, runbook, and rollout to a small set of pilot customers (opt-in)
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (internal): deploy to canary cluster behind feature flag; observe routing decisions on synthetic load
Phase 1 (pilot): opt-in pilot customers with no strict residency -> enable allowed-region fallback; monitor latency and correctness
Phase 2 (residency): invite 3 customers with strict residency; validate enforcement on zone drains via fault injection
Phase 3 (general): enable for all new Dedicated fleets, provide migration guide for existing fleets
Rollback: revert routing feature flag and release pool allocator fallback conserved tokens if regressions observed
metrics: P99 request latency by fleet and tier
Percent of requests served within configured latency_budget_ms
Number of routing decisions that would have violated residency (should be zero for strict mode)
Reservation utilization and reservation shortage events
Customer-facing error rate and incidents after rollout
risks: Incorrect residency label propagation could cause accidental data egress — mitigated by schema validation and a residency enforcement test suite
Overly aggressive expansion into remote pools could increase cost and tail latency for other customers — mitigated by rate-limiting expansions and cost alerts
Complexity increase in routing path could add CPU overhead on the router — mitigate by caching recent decisions and using lightweight scoring
Race between reservation token allocation and autoscaler leading to transient oversubscription — mitigate by two-phase allocation (reserve->confirm) and robust timeouts
